# Variance and standard deviation {#sec-variance}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}


::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Measuring (un)predictability
:::

Everyone has calculated their average grade to see if one passes of fail or get a mark, but, no one has ever check the variance of their grades!
While calculating the mean is well engrained, most probably don't remember the formula for variance or standard deviation.
And then when one performs test, we are forced to look at the variance without really understanding why. Test for homogeneity of variance or homoscedaisticy--what a fancy word. One is obviously because of lack of understanding of the test, but is the because we have been ignoring variance.

Due to familiarity and (usefuless) of the mean, we are comfortable comparing two numbers, and then inconsciously we assume that the distribution is the same. But a bit of thinking shold make us realize that mean is not the distribution and below is an example of three distributions with the same mean. Add uniform, normal and bimodal.

Likewise, if we just compare the variance, we would never assume the distribution are the same. So how can we compare distribution? a parsimonious approach is to both compare the mean and the variance. The mean gives the central tendency whereas the variance give the dispersion. For nicely behaving distribution (mostly unimodal and preferably symmetrical), those two metric is the minimum criteria (if we play long enough we can up with distribution with same mean and variance but )


## Formal {.unnumbered}

In the applied side, the equation for variance is

$var(X) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - \bar{X})^2$

Notice it is similar to the mean except that $X_i$ is replaced by $(X_i - \bar{X_i})^2$. If you stare long enough, it is square distance between the mean.
In other words, the variance is the average square distance.

With some algebra, you can see that

$$
  var(X) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i)^2 - (\bar{X})^2
$${#eq-varB}

If you want to do by hand the latter is simpler, but with a computer it is roughly the same.

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance squared

## Examples {.unnumbered}
 - `data = {1,1,1,1}`, mean = $\mu = 1$. The variance is

    $\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{4}\left((1 - \mu)^2 + (1 - \mu)^2 + (1 - \mu)^2 +(1 - \mu)^2 \right) = \frac{1}{4} 0^2 \times 4 = 0$
Tnis makes sense, there is not variance all numners are 1 so it makes sense the variance is 0.

- Imagine two schools: in one school all 20 students got 10/20,  in the other school, half of the students got 0/20 and the other half 20/20. While the means are the same 10/20, there is no variance in the first, and a variance of 100 in the second. Knowing the variance tells you the schools are different, while it might . You are more informed.

- In the example before
The mean was \
$\mu = \dfrac{1}{6}  5 + \frac{1}{6}  7 + \frac{2}{6}  10 + \frac{1}{6}  12 + \frac{1}{6} 14 = A number $ \

The variance is

$\sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{6}  (5 - \mu)^2 + \frac{1}{6}  (7 - \mu)^2 + \frac{2}{6}  (10 - \mu)^2  + \frac{1}{6}  (12 - \mu)^2 + \frac{1}{6} (14 - \mu)^2 = A number$

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Variance  represents the average dispersion around the mean. This dispersion is squared . Mostly because of distance, it has to be a positive number. But it is difficult to work with mathematically.
- Because of the square, we take the square root to have an intepratable value. Above, the variance of 100 of grades is meaningless if grades are beween 0 and 20. However, the standard deviation (10 = sqrt(100)) allows us to interpert in the proper scale.
- In the formal definition, @eq-varB, variance is number square and the mean. The square is called moment of order 2. We can also compute X^3 and more as higher moments and represent other geometry of the distribution.
- It is pointless to calculate the mean of one number, so does the calculation of the variance of two numbers.
- For the more advanced,a normal distribution is fully characterized by two numbers: the mean and the variance. In many distribution, which are nomral distrinution enough, comparing the two numbers should characterize the whole distribution and thus cimpare them.
- If you compute the variance of the data, it will divide by n-1 and not by n. While here we mostly divide by n, for most of one's life, it will divide by n-1. The division by n is called population variance (@sec-population), whereas the n-1 is sample variance. We will get back to it later but essentiallu, the n-1 is the best away to estimate the population variance which we do not know.

Just like the mean, the definition of variance in statistics is strictly divided between applied statistics (the descriptive measure of spread computed from a physical sample) and theoretical statistics (the expected squared deviation of a random variable from its population mean).
Here are the rigorous definitions for both, complete with textbook sources and raw LaTeX formatting.
1. Applied Statistics: The Sample Variance
In applied statistics, variance is a statistic used to measure the dispersion of an observed dataset. Crucially, the rigorous definition uses a divisor of n−1 (Bessel's correction) rather than n to ensure the sample variance is an unbiased estimator of the population variance.
Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Inference (2nd Edition, 2002)
Authors: George Casella and Roger L. Berger
Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning
The Definition

In Chapter 5 ("Properties of a Random Sample"), Casella and Berger
$S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - \bar{X})^2$

1. Theoretical Statistics: The Population Variance
In statistical theory, the variance of a random variable X is defined as the mathematical expectation of its squared distance from its theoretical mean (μ).
Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson
The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), the authors define the theoretical variance (often denoted as σ
2
  or Var(X)):
"Let X be a random variable with a finite mean μ=E[X]. The variance of X, denoted by σ
2
  or Var(X), is defined by
$\sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2]$
"

Depending on the underlying distribution of the variable, this expectation is evaluated using two distinct mathematical operations:
A. The Discrete Theoretical Case
If X is discrete with space D and probability mass function p(x):
$\sigma^2 = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} (x - \mu)^2 p(x)$

B. The Continuous Theoretical Case
If X is continuous with probability density function f(x):
$\sigma^2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x - \mu)^2 f(x) \, dx$



1. The Theoretical "Shortcut" Formula
In textbook proofs and algebraic manipulations, the theoretical definition is frequently re-expressed using a foundational identity derived from the linearity of expectation.

Textbook Source
Book: Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (3rd Edition, 2007)
Author: John A. Rice
Publisher: Cengage Learning
The Definition

In Chapter 4 ("Expected Values"), Rice demonstrates the standard computational theorem for variance:
"Theorem: If X has a finite mean μ, then
$\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2$

That is, the variance is the expected value of the square minus the square of the expected value." -->
